questions.q: The set of all possible values of $\theta$ in the interval $\left(0, \pi\right)$ for which the points $\left(1, 2\right) and  \left(sin\theta, cos\theta\right) lie on the same side of the line $x + y = 1$ is?$
questions.solution:
We know that if $A\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) \text{ and } B\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ lies on the same side to line $L = 0$, then ${L}_{A\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)}{L}_{B\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)} > 0$.

Given, the points $A\left(1, 2\right) \text{ and } B\left(sin\theta, cos\theta\right)$ lies on the same side of the line $x + y - 1 = 0$.

$∴ \left(1 + 2 - 1\right)\left(sin\theta + cos\theta - 1\right) > 0$

$⇒ sin\theta + cos\theta > 1$

$⇒ sin\theta \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + cos\theta \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 1 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ sin\theta . cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} + cos\theta . sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ sin\left(\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) > \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\pi}{4} < \left(\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) < \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

$⇒ 0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$⇒ \theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

questions.q: The locus of the mid-points of the perpendiculars drawn from points on the line $x = 2y$, to the line $x = y$, is.
questions.solution:
Slope of $PQ = \dfrac{k - \alpha}{h - 2\alpha} = - 1$
$k - \alpha = - h + 2\alpha ⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{h + k}{3} \ldots \left(1\right)
Also, $2h = 2\alpha + \beta$ and $2k = \alpha + \beta$
$2h = \alpha + 2k⇒ \alpha = 2h - 2k \ldots $\left(2\right)$
From $\left(1\right) \text{$ and }$\left(2\right),
\dfrac{h + k}{3} =$2$\left(h - k\right)$
So, locus is $6x - 6y = x + y ⇒ 5x = 7y$.

questions.q: A triangle has a vertex at $( 1, 2 )$ and the mid points of the two sides through it are $( - 1, 1 )$ and $( 2, 3 )$ . Then the centroid of this triangle is:
questions.solution:
Let co-ordinates of $B = \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$
$∴ \dfrac{{x}_{1} + 1}{2} = - 1 \text{ and } \dfrac{{y}_{1} + 2}{2} = 1$
$⇒ {x}_{1} = - 3, {y}_{1} = 0$
$∴ B = ( - 3, 0 )$
Let co-ordinates of $C = \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$
$∴ \dfrac{{x}_{2} + 1}{2} = 2 \text{ and } \dfrac{{y}_{2} + 2}{2} = 3$
$∴ C = \left(3, 4\right)$
Let centroid $G = \left(h, k\right)$
$h = \dfrac{1 + {x}_{1} + {x}_{2}}{3} = \dfrac{1 - 3 + 3}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
$k = \dfrac{2 + {y}_{1} + {y}_{2}}{3} = \dfrac{2 + 0 + 4}{3} = 2$
$∴$ Centroid, $G = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 2\right)$

questions.q: Lines are drawn parallel to the line $4x - 3y + 2 = 0,$ at a distance $\dfrac{3}{5}$ units  from the origin. Then which one of the following points lies on any of these lines?
questions.solution:
The equation of a line parallel to the line $ax + by + c = 0$ is $ax + by + k = 0 .$

Thus, the equation of a line parallel to $4x - 3y + 2 = 0$ is $4x - 3y + c = 0 .$

The distance of a line $ax + by + c = 0$ from origin is $\dfrac{\left|c\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}} .$

Given the line $4x - 3y + c = 0$ is at a distance of $\dfrac{3}{5}$ units from origin

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|c\right|}{\sqrt{16 + 9}} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|c\right|}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$⇒ c = \pm 3 .$

Hence, the equation of the lines are $4x - 3y + 3 = 0$ and $4x - 3y - 3 = 0 .$

Clearly point $\left(- \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ satisfy the given equation $4x - 3y + 3 = 0 .$

questions.q: If the two lines $x + \left(a - 1\right)y = 1$ and $2x + {a}^{2}y = 1, \left(a \in R - \left\{0,1\right\}\right)$ are perpendicular, then the distance of their point of intersection from the origin is
questions.solution:
If two lines ${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y = {c}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y = {c}_{2}$ are perpendicular, then ${a}_{1}{a}_{2} + {b}_{1}{b}_{2} = 0 .$

Since, given lines $x + \left(a - 1\right)y = 1$ and $2x + {a}^{2}y = 1$ are perpendicular, hence, we get

$1 ⋅ 2 + \left(a - 1\right) ⋅ {a}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ {a}^{3} - {a}^{2} + 2 = 0$

$⇒ \left(a + 1\right) ⋅ \left({a}^{2} - 2a + 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ a = - 1$ or ${a}^{2} - 2a + 2 = 0$

But, the discriminant of the quadratic equation is ${\left(- 2\right)}^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times 2 = 4 - 8 = - 4,$ hence, no real roots exist.

Thus, the only possible value of $a$ is $- 1 .$

And, hence the lines are $x - 2y = 1$ and $2x + y = 1 .$

Point of intersection of these two lines is $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}, - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)$

We know that, the distance of a point $\left(x, y\right)$ from origin is $\sqrt{{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}$
Hence, distance of the point $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}, - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)$ from origin $= \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{25} + \dfrac{1}{25}}$= \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}} .$

questions.q: Slope of a line passing through $P ( 2, 3 )$ and intersecting the line $x + y = 7$ at a distance of $4$ units from $P,$ is
questions.solution:
Given, the point $P\left(2, 3\right)$ on the line $x + y = 7 .$

Let, the point of intersection of the two lines be $Q$

Then, $Q$ can be taken as $Q ≡ ( \alpha, 7 - \alpha )$

Given, $PQ = 4$ units and the distance between the points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) \text{ and } \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is $\sqrt{{\left({x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left({y}_{1} - {y}_{2}\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \sqrt{( \alpha - {2 )}^{2} + {\left(7 - \alpha - 3\right)}^{2}} = 4$

$⇒ \sqrt{( \alpha - {2 )}^{2} + {\left(4 - \alpha\right)}^{2}} = 4$

$⇒ ( \alpha - {2 )}^{2} + {\left(4 - \alpha\right)}^{2} = {4}^{2}$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2} - 4\alpha + 4 + 16 - 8\alpha + {\alpha}^{2} = 16$

$⇒ 2{\alpha}^{2} - 12\alpha + 4 = 0$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2} - 6\alpha + 2 = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{- \left(- 6\right) \pm \sqrt{{\left(- 6\right)}^{2} - 4 \times 1 \times 2}}{2 \times 2}$

$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 8}}{4}$

$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{4}$

$⇒ \alpha = 3 \pm \sqrt{7}$

The slope of a line joining the points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) \text{ and } \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is $\dfrac{{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}}{{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}} .$

If we take $\alpha = 3 - \sqrt{7},$ then $Q ≡ \left(3 - \sqrt{7}, 4 + \sqrt{7}\right)$

And, the slope of $PQ = m = \dfrac{4 + \sqrt{7} - 3}{3 - \sqrt{7} - 2} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{7}}{1 - \sqrt{7}}$

If we take $\alpha = 3 + \sqrt{7},$ then $Q ≡ \left(3 + \sqrt{7}, 4 - \sqrt{7}\right)$

And, the slope of $PQ = m = \dfrac{4 - \sqrt{7} - 3}{3 + \sqrt{7} - 2} = \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{7}}{1 + \sqrt{7}} .$

questions.q: Suppose that the points $\left(h, k\right), \left(1, 2\right)$ and $\left(- 3, 4\right) lie on the line${L}_{1} .$ If a line ${L}_{2}passing through the $points \left(h, k\right) and \left(4, 3\right) is perpendicular to${L}_{1},$ then \dfrac{k}{h} e$quals:
questions.solution:
Slope of line ${L}_{1}$ is $\dfrac{4 - 2}{- 3 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{- 4} = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$
Hence slope of ${L}_{2}$ is $2 .$
From line ${L}_{1}, \dfrac{k - 2}{h - 1} = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$
$⇒ h + 2k = 5$ …..(1)
From line ${L}_{2}, \dfrac{k - 3}{h - 4} = 2$
$⇒ k = 2h - 5$ ..…(2)
From (1) and (2) $h = 3$ and $k = 1$
$⇒ \dfrac{k}{h} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.q: If a straight line passing through the point $P\left(- 3, 4\right)$ is such that its intercepted portion between the coordinate axes is bisected at $P$, then its equation is :
questions.solution:
Let the line passing through $\left(- 3, 4\right)$ intersect the coordinate axes at A$ & $B$.

By mid-point formula, co-ordinates of $P$\left(\dfrac{\alpha + 0}{2}, \dfrac{0 + \beta}{2}\right)$.

Comparing with given co-ordinate values, we get

$\dfrac{\alpha + 0}{2} = - 3 ⇒ \alpha = - 6$

and $\dfrac{\beta + 0}{2} = 4 ⇒ \beta = 8$

Hence, equation of line is $\dfrac{x}{- 6} + \dfrac{y}{8} = 1$

$⇒ 4x - 3y + 24 = 0$

questions.q: If the straight line $2x - 3y + 17 = 0$ is perpendicular to the line passing through the points $\left(7, 17\right) and \left(15, \beta\right), then $\beta$ equals :$
questions.solution:
Slope of line $2x - 3y + 17 = 0$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

Slope of a line passing through $\left(7, 17\right) and \left(15, \beta\right) is \dfrac{17 - \beta}{7 - 15}.

Since, both lines are perpendicular to each other, so product of slopes will be $- 1$.

$⇒ $\dfrac{17 - \beta}{7 - 15} \times \dfrac{2}{3} =$- 1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{17 - \beta}{- 8} =- \dfrac{3}{2}$ ⇒ 17 - \beta = 12 ⇒ \beta = 5$.

$

questions.q: In a triangle, the sum of lengths of two sides is $\mathrm{x}$ and the product of the lengths of the same two sides is $y$. if $x^{2}-c^{2}=y,$ where $c$ is the length of the third side of the triangle, then the circumradius of the triangle is
questions.solution:
Let two sides of triangle are $a and b$.



$\begin{aligned}$& a+b=x \\

& a b=y \\

& x^{2}-c^{2}=y \Rightarrow(a+b)^{2}-c^{2}=a b \\

\Rightarrow &(a+b-c)(a+b+c)=a b \\

\Rightarrow & 2(s-c)(2 s)=a b \\

\Rightarrow & 4 s(s-c)=a b \\

\Rightarrow & $\frac{s(s-c)}{a b}=\frac{1}{4}$\\

\Rightarrow & \cos ^{2} $\frac{c}{2}=\frac{1}{4}$\\

\Rightarrow & \cos c=-$\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow$c=120^{{}^{\circ}}

\end{aligned}



$\therefore$ Area of triangle is,

$\Delta=\frac{1}{2} a b\left(\sin 120^{{}^{\circ}}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} a b\because \quad R=\frac{a b c}{4 \Delta}\because \quad \mathrm{R}=\frac{a b c}{\sqrt{3} a b}=\frac{c}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.q: If the line $3x + 4y - 24 = 0$ intersects the $x$-axis is at the point $A$ and the $y$-axis at the point $B,$ then the incentre of the triangle $OAB,$ where $O$is the origin, is:
questions.solution:
The $x$ intercept of the line $3x + 4y - 24 = 0$ can be obtained by putting $y = 0$ i.e. $3x - 24 = 0$

$⇒ x = 8$

Hence, the point $A$ is $\left(8, 0\right) .$

Now, the $y$ intercept of the line $3x + 4y - 24 = 0$ can be obtained by putting $x = 0$ i.e. $4y - 24 = 0$

$⇒ y = 6$

Hence, the point $B$ is $\left(0, 6\right) .$

In $∆ OAB,$ we have $OA = b = 8, OB = a = 6$ and $AB = c = \sqrt{{\left(8 - 0\right)}^{2} + {\left(0 - 6\right)}^{2}} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$ units.

And, we know that the co-ordinates of incentre $I$ of a triangle with vertices $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right), \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ and $\left({x}_{3}, {y}_{3}\right)$ and having length of the sides opposite to these vertices as $a, b$ and $c,$ respectively, is

$I ≡ \left(\dfrac{a{x}_{1} + b{x}_{2} + c{x}_{3}}{a + b + c}, \dfrac{a{y}_{1} + b{y}_{2} + c{y}_{3}}{a + b + c}\right)$

$⇒ I ≡ \left(\dfrac{6\left(8\right) + 8\left(0\right) + 10\left(0\right)}{24}, \dfrac{6\left(0\right) + 8\left(6\right) + 10\left(0\right)}{24}\right)$

$⇒ I = \left(2, 2\right) .$

questions.q: A point $P$ moves on the line $2x - 3y + 4 = 0 .$ If $Q\left(1, 4\right)$ and $R\left(3, - 2\right)$ are fixed points, then the locus of the centroid of $\DeltaPQR$ is a line:
questions.solution:
Let, coordinate of centroid is $( h, k )$ and coordinate of point $P$ is $( \alpha, \beta )$

We know that the centroid of a triangle with vertices $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right), \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right) and \left({x}_{3}, {y}_{3}\right) is \left(\dfrac{{x}_{1} + {x}_{2} + {x}_{3}}{3}, \dfrac{{y}_{1} + {y}_{2} + {y}_{3}}{3}\right) .

Hence,$ in ∆ PQR,$ we have \dfrac{\alpha + 1 + 3}{3} =$h and $\dfrac{\beta + 4 - 2}{3} =k$

$⇒ \alpha = 3h - 4, \beta = 3k - 2$

Since $( \alpha, \beta )$ lies on the line $2x - 3y + 4 = 0$

Hence, $2\left(3h - 4\right) - 3\left(3k - 2\right) + 4 = 0$

$⇒ 6h - 9k + 2 = 0$

For finding the locus replace $\left(h, k\right)$ by $\left(x, y\right)$

Hence, the locus of centroid is $6x - 9y + 2 = 0$ which has slope $= - \dfrac{6}{\left(- 9\right)$} = $\dfrac{2}{3} since$ the slope of a lineax + by + c = 0$ is $- $\dfrac{a}{b} .

$

$⇒ $\left(\sqrt{2}x + y\right)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}x - y}{- 4\sqrt{2}}\right) = 4\sqrt{2}$

$⇒ e = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{16}{32}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$ and length of transverse axis

$= 8\sqrt{2}$.

Equation of the line, which is perpendicular to the line, $3 x+y=\lambda(\lambda \neq 0)$ and passing through origin, is given by

$\frac{x-0}{3}=\frac{y-0}{1}=$ r

r=$\frac{-((3 \times 0)+(1 \times 0)-\lambda)}{3^2+1^2}=\frac{\lambda}{10}$So, foot of perpendicular $P= \left(\frac{3 \lambda}{10}, \frac{\lambda}{10}\right)

 \text{ Now, }$ P A=$\sqrt{\left(\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{3 \lambda}{10}\right)^2+\left(0-\frac{\lambda}{10}\right)^2}\\

questions.solution:
Let the coordinate $A$ be $(0, c)$
Equations of the given lines are
$x-y+2=0 and 7 x-y+3=0$
We know that the diagonals of the rhombus will be parallel to the angle bisectors of the two given lines; $y=x+2 and y=7 x+3\therefore$ equation of angle bisectors is given as:

$\begin{aligned}$&$\frac{x-y+2}{\sqrt{2}}=\pm \frac{7 x-y+3}{5 \sqrt{2}}$\\
&5 x-5 y+10=$\pm($7 x-y+3)
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ Parallel equations of the diagonals are $2 x+4 y-7=0 and 12 x-6 y+13=0\therefore$ slopes of diagonals are $\frac{-1}{2}$ and 2 .
Now, slope of the diagonal from $A(0, \mathrm{c})$ and passing through $P(1,2)$ is $(2-c)$
\therefore 2-c=2 \Rightarrow c=0 $\text{ (not possible) }

\therefore$2-c=$\frac{-1}{2} \Rightarrow$c=$\frac{5}{2}

\therefore \text{ ordinate$ of $A is } \frac{5}{2} \text{. }$

questions.q: The locus of the point of intersection of the straight lines, $tx - 2y - 3t = 0$ and $x - 2ty + 3 = 0\left(t \in R\right),$ is:
options: A hyperbola with the length of conjugate axis 3
An ellipse with the length of major axis 6
questions.solution:
$tx - 2y - 3t = 0 . . . . . . . \left(1\right)

$x - 2ty + 3 = 0 . . . . . . $\left(2\right)$ ,

Multiply by $t$ and subtract from above equation, we get

$y\left(2{t}^{2} - 2\right) = 6t$

Now multiply by $t$ in first equation and subtract second, we get

$\left({t}^{2} - 1\right)x = 3 \left({t}^{2} - 1\right)$

$⇒ x = 3\dfrac{{( t}^{2} + 1 )}{{t}^{2} - 1}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{9} = {\left(\dfrac{{t}^{2} + 1}{{t}^{2} - 1}\right)}^{2} \text{$ and $} \dfrac{2y}{3} = \dfrac{2t}{{t}^{2} - 1}$

$⇒ \dfrac{4{y}^{2}}{9} = \dfrac{4{t}^{2}}{{\left({t}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{9} - \dfrac{4{y}^{2}}{9} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{9} - \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{\dfrac{9}{4}} = 1$

${a}^{2} = 9; ⇒ a=3$

${b}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4}⇒ b = \dfrac{3}{2}$
$∴$ Length of conjugate axis $= 2b = 2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} = 3$

Length of transverse axis$= 2a = 6$

${e}^{2} = 1 + \dfrac{\dfrac{9}{4}}{9} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{4}; e = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$

questions.q: Let $k$ be an integer such that the triangle with vertices $\left(k, - 3k\right), \left(5, k\right) and \left(- k, 2\right) has area $28$ sq. units. Then the orthocenter of this triangle is at the point:$
questions.solution:
​​​​​​​

Given, Area of the triangle $∆ ABC = 28$\to \dfrac{1}{2}\left|k\left(k - 2\right) + 5\left(2 + 3k\right) - k\left(- 4k\right)\right| = 28$

$\to \left|k\left(k - 2\right) + 5\left(2 + 3k\right) - k\left(- 4k\right)\right| = 56$

$\to 5{k}^{2} + 13k − 46 = 0$

$\to k = 2$ and $k = - \dfrac{23}{5}$ (Not possible)

Altitude from $A: x = 2$

Altitude from $B: y - 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(x - 5\right)$

So, their point of intersection is $H\left(2, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

questions.q: A straight line through origin $O$ meets the lines $3y = 10 - 4x$and $8x + 6y + 5 = 0$ at points $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then, $O$ divides the segment $AB$ in the ratio
questions.solution:
Let $A\left({r}_{1}cos\theta, {r}_{1}sin\theta\right)$

$A$ Lies on straight line $4x + 3y = 10$

$⇒ 4\left({r}_{1}cos\theta\right) + 3\left({r}_{1}sin\theta\right) = 10$

$⇒ {r}_{1}\left(4cos\theta + 3sin\theta\right) = 10$
$⇒ {r}_{1} = \dfrac{10}{4cos\theta + 3sin\theta}$

Let $B\left(- {r}_{2}cos\theta, - {r}_{2}sin\theta\right)$

$B$ lies on line $8x + 6y + 5 = 0$

$⇒ 8\left(- {r}_{2}cos\theta\right) + 6\left(- {r}_{2}sin\theta\right) + 5 = 0$

$⇒ {r}_{2}\left(8cos\theta + 6sin\theta\right) - 5 = 0$⇒ {r}_{2} = \dfrac{5}{8cos\theta + 6sin\theta}$
$∴ \dfrac{{r}_{1}}{{r}_{2}} = \dfrac{4}{1}$

questions.q: A ray of light is incident along a line which meets another line $7x - y + 1 = 0$ at the point $\left(0, 1\right)$. The ray is then reflected from this point along the line $y + 2x = 1$. Then the equation of the line of incidence of the ray of light is :
questions.solution:
Let slope of incident ray be $m .$

$∴$ angle of incidence $=$ angle of reflection

$∴$\left|\dfrac{m - 7}{1 + 7m}\right| = \left|\dfrac{- 2 - 7}{1 - 14}\right| = \dfrac{9}{13}$

$⇒ \dfrac{m - 7}{1 + 7m} = \dfrac{9}{13}or\dfrac{m - 7}{1 + 7m} = - \dfrac{9}{13}$

$⇒ 13m - 91 = 9 + 63m$, or$13m - 91 = - 9 - 63m$

$⇒$m = -2$ or $m = \dfrac{41}{38}$

$⇒ y - 1 = \dfrac{41}{38}\left(x - 0\right)$

$⇒$38y - 38 - 41x = 0$

questions.solution:
${L}_{1}: 4x + 3y - 12 = 0$

${L}_{2}: 3x + 4y - 12 = 0$

${L}_{1} + \lambda{L}_{2} = 0$

$⇒$\left(4x + 3y - 12\right) + \lambda\left(3x + 4y - 12\right) = 0$

$⇒$x\left(4 + 3\lambda\right) + y\left(3 + 4\lambda\right) - 12\left(1 + \lambda\right) = 0$

Point $A\left(\dfrac{12\left(1 + \lambda\right)}{4 + 3\lambda}, 0\right)$

Point $B\left(0, \dfrac{12\left(1 + \lambda\right)}{3 + 4\lambda}\right)$

Mid point $⇒ h = \dfrac{6\left(1 + \lambda\right)}{4 + 3\lambda}$ .......$\left(i\right)$

$k = \dfrac{6\left(1 + \lambda\right)}{3 + 4\lambda}$ .......$\left(ii\right)$

Eliminate $\lambda$ from equations $\left(i\right)$ and $\left(ii\right)$ then

$6\left(h + k\right) = 7hk$

Hence, locus is

$6\left(x + y\right) = 7xy$

questions.q: The point $\left(2, 1\right)$ is translated parallel to the line $L: x - y = 4$ by $2\sqrt{3}$ units. If the new point $Q$ lies in the third quadrant, then the equation of the line passing through $Q$ and perpendicular to $L$ is
questions.solution:
Equation of line $QR$ perpendicular to $L: x - y = 4$ is
$x + y - c = 0 \ldots \left(1\right)$

Distance of $QR$ from $\left(2, 1\right)$ is $2\sqrt{3}$

$⇒ 2\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\left|2 + 1 - c\right|}{\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ 2\sqrt{6} = \left|3 - c\right|$

$⇒ c - 3 = \pm 2\sqrt{6} ⇒ c = 3 \pm 2\sqrt{6}$

Line can be $x + y = 3 \pm 2\sqrt{6}$

$x + y = 3 - 2\sqrt{6}$ (since $Q$ is in the third quadrant)

questions.q: Locus of the image of the point $( 2, 3 )$ in the line $\left(2 x - 3 y + 4\right) + k \left(x - 2 y + 3\right) = 0 , k \in R ,$ is a
questions.solution:
Let image is $( \alpha, \beta )$

$∴$ point $( \dfrac{2 + \alpha}{2} , \dfrac{3 + \beta}{2} )$ lies on the given variable line.

$∴ 2( \dfrac{2 + \alpha}{2} ) - 3( \dfrac{3 + \beta}{2} ) + 4 + k( \dfrac{2 + \alpha}{2} - 2 \times \dfrac{3 + \beta}{2} + 3 ) = 0$

$⇒ 2\alpha - 3\beta + 3 + k( \alpha - 2\beta + 2 ) = 0 . . . . . . . \left(1\right)

again, product$ of two slopes= - 1$

$⇒ $\dfrac{3 - \beta}{2 - \alpha}$ \times $\dfrac{2 + k}{3 + 2k} =$- 1$

$⇒ 6 - 2\beta + k( 3 - \beta ) = - ( 6 - 3\alpha ) - k( 4 - 2\alpha )$

$⇒ k ( 7 - 2\alpha - \beta ) = 3\alpha + 2\beta - 12$

$⇒ k = $\dfrac{3\alpha + 2\beta - 12}{7 - 2\alpha - \beta}

Substituting value$ of k$ in ,\left(1\right) we get

$2\alpha - 3\beta + 3 + $\dfrac{3\alpha + 2\beta + - 12}{7 - 2\alpha - \beta}$ ( \alpha - 2\beta + 2 ) = 0$

$⇒ 14\alpha - 4{\alpha}^{2} - 2\alpha\beta - 21\beta + 6\alpha\beta + 3{\beta}^{2} + 21 - 6\alpha - 3\beta + 3{\alpha}^{2} - 6\alpha\beta + 6\alpha + 2\alpha\beta - 4{\beta}^{2} + 4\beta - 12\alpha + 24\beta - 24 = 0$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} - 2a - 4\beta + 3 = 0$

$∴$ Locus is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2x - 4y + 3 = 0$

Which is a circle with radius $= \sqrt{1 + 4 - 3} = \sqrt{2}$
$

questions.q: If a line $L$ is perpendicular to the line $5x - y = 1,$ and the area of the triangle formed by the line $L$ and the coordinate axes is $5$ sq units, then the distance of the line $L$ from the line $x + 5y = 0$ is
questions.solution:
The equation of a line perpendicular to the line $ax + by + c = 0$ is $bx - ay + k = 0, k \in R .$

Given, line $L$ is perpendicular to $5x - y = 1,$ hence the equation of $L$ is $x +5 y + k =0$

For finding $x$-Intercept, put $y = 0$

$⇒ x + k = 0, ⇒ x = - k$

$∴$x$-intercept$= - k$

Similarly, for finding $y$- Intercept, put $x = 0$

$⇒ 5y + k = 0, ⇒ y = - \dfrac{k}{5}$

$∴$y$-intercept$= - \dfrac{k}{5}$

Given, the area formed by the line $L$ with the coordinate axes is $5$ sq units.

Hence, the area of $\text{\Delta =}\dfrac{1}{2} \times \left(- k\right)\left(- \dfrac{k}{5}\right) = 5$

$⇒ {k}^{2} = 50$

$⇒ k = \pm \text{5}\sqrt{2}$

Hence, the equation of the line is $L: x ⁡+5 y ⁡ \pm 5 \sqrt{2} = 0$

Now, we know that the distance between the parallel lines $ax + by + c = 0$ and $ax + by + {c}_{1} = 0$ is $\dfrac{\left|c - {c}_{1}\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}$

Thus, the distance between the lines $x +5 y =0$ and $x +5 y\text{⁡ \pm 5}\sqrt{2} = 0$ is

$d = \left|\dfrac{\pm 5\sqrt{2} - 0}{\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {5}^{2}}}\right|$

$⇒ d = \dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{26}}$

$⇒ d = \dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{13 \times 2}} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{13}}$ units.

questions.q: The circumcentre of a triangle lies at the origin and its centroid is the midpoint of the line segment joining the points ( {a}^{2} + 1, {a}^{2} + 1 ) and $\left(2a , - 2 a\right), a \ne 0$. Then for any $a,$ the orthocentre of this triangle lies on the line
questions.solution:
The mid-point of a line segment joining the points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ and $\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is $\left(\dfrac{{x}_{1} + {x}_{2}}{2}, \dfrac{{y}_{1} + {y}_{2}}{2}\right)$

Given, the centroid $G$ is the mid-point of the line segment joining the points $\left({a}^{2} + 1, {a}^{2} + 1\right)$ and $\left(2a, - 2a\right)$, thus $G ≡ \left(\dfrac{{a}^{2} + 1 + 2a}{2}, \dfrac{{a}^{2} + 1 - 2a}{2}\right)$

$⇒ G ≡ \left(\dfrac{{\left(a + 1\right)}^{2}}{2}, \dfrac{{\left(a - 1\right)}^{2}}{2}\right) .$

Also, given circumcentre $C$ is origin $⇒ C ≡ \left(0, 0\right) .$

We know that, for a triangle circumcentre, orthocentre and centroid are collinear.

Thus, $C, G$ and orthocentre $H$ are collinear.

Again, we know that the equation of a line passing through the points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ and $\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is $y - {y}_{1} = \left(\dfrac{{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}}{{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}}\right)\left(x - {x}_{1}\right)$

Thus, the orthocentre lies on the line joining the points $\left(0, 0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{{\left(a + 1\right)}^{2}}{2}, \dfrac{{\left(a - 1\right)}^{2}}{2}\right)$ and its equation, is

$y - 0 = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{{\left(a - 1\right)}^{2}}{2} - 0\right)}{\left(\dfrac{{\left(a + 1\right)}^{2}}{2} - 0\right)}\left(x - 0\right)$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{{\left(a - 1\right)}^{2}}{{\left(a + 1\right)}^{2}}\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {\left(a - 1\right)}^{2}x - {\left(a + 1\right)}^{2}y = 0 .$

$\begin{aligned}
&x+2 a y+a=0 \\
&x+3 b y+b=0 \\
&x+4 a y+a=0
\end{aligned}$

Subtracting equation (3) from (1)

$\begin{aligned}
&-2 a y=0 \\
&a y=0 \Rightarrow y=0
\end{aligned}$

Putting value of $y in $equation (1), we get

$\begin{aligned}
&x+0+a=0 \\
&x=-a
\end{aligned}$

Putting value of$x and y in $equation (2), we get

$\begin{aligned}
&-a+b=0 \\
&a=b
\end{aligned}$

Thus,$(a, b)$ lies on a straight line

$∴ 3bc - 2ad =0$

questions.q:
If two lines $L_1 and L_2$ in space, are defined by

$\begin{aligned}$& L_1=\{x=$\sqrt{\lambda}$y+($\sqrt{\lambda}-$1), \\
& \quad z=($\sqrt{\lambda}-$1) y+$\sqrt{\lambda}$\} $\text{$ and }\\
& L_2=\{x=$\sqrt{\mu}$y+(1-$\sqrt{\mu}),
\end{aligned}$z=(1-$\sqrt{\mu})$y+$\sqrt{\mu}$\}

then $L_1$ is perpendicular to $L_2$, for all nonnegative reals $\lambda and \mu$, such that :
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{L}_1$,

$\begin{aligned}$& x=$\sqrt{\lambda}$y+($\sqrt{\lambda}-$1) \Rightarrow y=$\frac{x-(\sqrt{\lambda}-1)}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$\\
& z=($\sqrt{\lambda}-$1) y+$\sqrt{\lambda} \Rightarrow$y=$\frac{z-\sqrt{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\lambda}-1}
\end{aligned}$From (i) and (ii)

$\frac{x-(\sqrt{\lambda}-1)}{\sqrt{\lambda}}=\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-\sqrt{\lambda}}{\sqrt{\lambda}-1}$The equation (A) is the equation of line $\mathrm{L}_1$. Similarly equation of line $\mathrm{L}_2$ is

$\frac{x-(1-\sqrt{\mu})}{\sqrt{\mu}}=\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-\sqrt{\mu}}{1-\sqrt{\mu}}$Since $\mathrm{L}_1 \perp \mathrm{L}_2$, therefore

$\begin{aligned}$& $\sqrt{\lambda} \sqrt{\mu}+$1 $\times$1+($\sqrt{\lambda}-$1)(1-$\sqrt{\mu})=$0 \\
& \Rightarrow $\sqrt{\lambda}+\sqrt{\mu}=$0 \Rightarrow $\sqrt{\lambda}=-\sqrt{\mu}$\\
& \Rightarrow \lambda=\mu
\end{aligned}

questions.q: If the $x$-intercept of some line $L$ is double as that of the line, $3 x+4 y=12$ and the $y$-intercept of $L$ is half as that of the same line, then the slope of $L$ is :
questions.solution:
Given line $3 x+4 y=12$ can be rewritten as

$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{3 x}{12}+\frac{4 y}{12}=$1 \Rightarrow $\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{3}=$1 \\
& \Rightarrow x $\text{-intercept }=$4 $\text{$ and }y $\text{-intercept }=$3
\end{aligned}

Let$ the required line be\mathrm{L}: \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1$ where
$a=x$-intercept and $b=y$-intercept
According to the question
$a=4 \times 2=8 and b=3 / 2\therefore$ Required line is $\frac{x}{8}+\frac{2 y}{3}=1\Rightarrow 3 x+16 y=24\Rightarrow y=\frac{-3}{16} x+\frac{24}{16}$
Hence, required slope =$\frac{-3}{16}.$

questions.q: The acute angle between two lines such that the direction cosines $l, m, n$, of each of them satisfy the equations $l+m+n=0$ and $l^2+m^2-n^2=0$ is :
questions.solution:
Let $l_1, m_1, n_1$ and $l_2, m_2, n_2$ be the d.c of line 1 and 2 respectively, then as given $l_1+m_1+n_1=0$
and $l_2+m_2+n_2=0$
and $l_1{ }^2+m_1{ }^2-n_1^2=0$ and $l_2^2+m_2^2-n_2^2=0   \left(\becausel+m+n=0\right.$ and $\left.l^2+m²-n²=0\right)$
Angle between lines, \thetais

\cos $\theta=$ l_1 l_2+m_1 m_2+n_1 n_2

As given $ l^2+m²=n²$ and $l+m=-n\Rightarrow(-n)^2-2 l m=n² \Rightarrow 2 l m=0$ or $l m=0$
So $l_1 m_1=0, l_2 m_2=0$
If $l_1=0, m_1  ≠ 0$ then $l_1 m_2=0$
If $m_1=0, l_1  ≠ 0$ then $l_2 m_1=0$
If $l_2=0, m_2  ≠ 0$ then $l_2 m_1=0$
If $m_2=0, l_2  ≠ 0$ then $l_1 m_2=0$
Also $l_1 l_2=0$ and $m_1 m_2=0
\begin{aligned}
& l²+m²-n²=l²+m²+n²-2 n²=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 1-2 n²=0 \Rightarrow n=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\
& \therefore n_1=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, n_2=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\
& \therefore \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \theta=60^{{}^{\circ}} \text{ (acute angle) }
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The point of intersection of the lines $\left(a^3+3\right) x+a y+a-3=0$ and $\left(a^5+2\right) x+(a+2) y+2 a+3=0$ (a real) lies on the $y$-axis for
options:
no value of $a$

more than two values of $a$

exactly one value of $a$

exactly two values of $a$
questions.solution:
Given equation of lines are $\left(a^3+3\right) x+a y+a-3=0$ and $\left(a^5+2\right) x+(a+2) y+2 a+3=0$ (a real)
Since point of intersection of lines lies on $\mathrm{y}$-axis.
$\therefore$ Put $x=0$ in each equation, we get $a \mathrm{y}+a-3=0 and (a+2) y+2 a+3=0$
On solving these we get

$\begin{aligned}$& (a+2)(a-3)-a(2 a+3)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow a²-a-6-2 a²-3 a=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-a²-4 a-6=0 \Rightarrow a²+4 a+6=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a=$\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16-24}}{2}=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{-8}}{2}$\\
& ($\text{ not real) }
\end{aligned}$This shows that the point of intersection of the lines lies on the $y$-axis for no value of ' $a$ '.
